questions.stem: A client has a chest tube to wet suction for a pneumothorax. Yesterday the water seal chamber bubbled only when the client coughed. Today the nurse sees continuous bubbling in the water seal chamber, and the client's breathing is unchanged. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Document the bubbling as an expected sign that air is leaving the chest
Look for an air leak, from the dressing along the tubing
Clamp the chest tube close to the chest and leave it clamped
Turn up the wall suction until the bubbling settles

rationale.correct: Intermittent bubbling in the water seal can be expected while air leaves the chest; new continuous bubbling means an air leak in the client or the system.

perOption.a: Intermittent bubbling with coughing can be expected; new continuous bubbling is not.
perOption.b: Continuous bubbling means air is entering the system; the nurse checks the insertion site and connections to find the leak.
perOption.c: Clamping can cause a tension pneumothorax; brief clamping is done only to locate a leak, per policy.
perOption.d: More suction does not fix a leak.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to an air leak in a chest drainage system.

questions.stem: While a client is being helped into a chair, the chest tube separates from the drainage system tubing. The client is breathing comfortably. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Clamp the chest tube with a hemostat until a new system is set up
Put the tube end 2 to 4 cm under sterile water
Remove the chest tube and cover the site
Wrap the open end of the tube in sterile gauze

rationale.correct: If a chest tube disconnects, create a water seal right away, then connect a new sterile system.

perOption.a: Clamping for long risks a tension pneumothorax.
perOption.b: This creates a temporary water seal that keeps air from entering the chest.
perOption.c: The tube should not be removed.
perOption.d: Gauze does not create a seal.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage a disconnected chest tube.

questions.stem: A confused client pulls out a chest tube that was placed for a pneumothorax. The nurse arrives within seconds and hears air moving at the site. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Reinsert the chest tube through the same opening, using sterile gloves
Cover the site with a sterile dressing taped on three sides
Leave the site open to air and call the provider
Apply a fully sealed occlusive dressing on all four sides

rationale.correct: Cover the site with a sterile dressing taped on three sides, assess for respiratory distress and notify the provider.

perOption.a: Only a provider inserts a chest tube.
perOption.b: A three-sided dressing lets air escape but stops air from entering.
perOption.c: An open site lets air into the pleural space.
perOption.d: A fully sealed dressing can trap air and cause a tension pneumothorax.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond when a chest tube comes out.

questions.stem: A client has a chest tube connected to wet suction after a thoracotomy. Which actions are appropriate when caring for this client? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the drainage system below the level of the chest
Keep the tubing free of dependent loops
Expect the water level in the water seal to rise and fall with breathing
Clamp the tube whenever the client is moved or walked
Strip or milk the tubing every hour to keep it open

rationale.correct: Chest tube care: keep the system below the chest, avoid loops, expect tidaling, and do not clamp or strip routinely.

perOption.a: Gravity prevents backflow into the pleural space.
perOption.b: Loops collect fluid and slow drainage.
perOption.c: Tidaling shows the system is working and the lung is not fully expanded.
perOption.d: Routine clamping risks a tension pneumothorax.
perOption.e: Routine stripping creates high negative pressure and is done only if prescribed.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Care for a client with a chest tube.

questions.stem: The nurse is checking the chest drainage system of a client 6 hours after a lobectomy. For each chamber, select the finding that requires follow-up.

options.text: 150 mL of bright red drainage in the last hour
40 mL of serosanguineous drainage over 8 hours
Water level rises and falls with breathing
Constant bubbling
Gentle, continuous bubbling
No bubbling with the wall suction on

rationale.correct: Know what is expected in each chamber of a chest drainage system and what needs follow-up.

perOption.a: More than about 100 mL/hr of bright red drainage suggests hemorrhage.
perOption.b: This is expected drainage.
perOption.c: Tidaling is expected.
perOption.d: Continuous bubbling indicates an air leak.
perOption.e: This shows the suction is working.
perOption.f: No bubbling means the suction is not working, for example from a loose connection or low setting.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Assess a chest drainage system.

questions.stem: After a high-speed car crash, a 34-year-old driver has severe shortness of breath, absent breath sounds on the left and a trachea that has shifted to the right. The blood pressure is 74/40 mm Hg and the neck veins are distended. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Left tension pneumothorax
Right simple pneumothorax
Left pulmonary contusion
Cardiac tamponade

rationale.correct: Tension pneumothorax is an emergency treated with needle decompression, then a chest tube.

perOption.a: Air trapped in the left chest pushes the trachea and mediastinum to the right and lowers cardiac output.
perOption.b: The trachea shifts away from a tension pneumothorax, and here the absent sounds are on the left.
perOption.c: A contusion does not shift the trachea or cause JVD.
perOption.d: Tamponade causes JVD and hypotension but not absent breath sounds or tracheal shift.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize a tension pneumothorax.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old client has several fractured ribs on the right after falling down stairs. The client is short of breath with an SpO2 of 90%. Which finding suggests a flail chest?

options.text: A chest segment that sinks in as the client breathes in
A barrel-shaped chest with a wide front-to-back diameter
A crackling feeling under the skin around the injury
Dullness when the right lower chest is percussed

rationale.correct: Flail chest happens when several adjacent ribs break in more than one place; the segment moves opposite to the rest of the chest.

perOption.a: Paradoxical movement of a chest wall segment is the sign of flail chest.
perOption.b: This is associated with COPD.
perOption.c: This is subcutaneous emphysema.
perOption.d: This suggests fluid or blood in the chest.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize flail chest.

questions.stem: The high-pressure alarm sounds on a client's ventilator. The client is coughing, the SpO2 has fallen from 96% to 92%, and the nurse hears coarse rhonchi over the trachea. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Suction the client's airway
Silence the alarm and recheck in 15 minutes
Check the circuit for a disconnection
Increase the set tidal volume by 100 mL

rationale.correct: High-pressure alarms come from obstruction (secretions, kinks, biting, coughing, bronchospasm); low-pressure alarms come from leaks or disconnections.

perOption.a: Secretions raise airway pressure; suctioning clears them.
perOption.b: Alarms must be investigated, not just silenced.
perOption.c: Disconnections cause low-pressure alarms.
perOption.d: This would raise the pressure further.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a high-pressure ventilator alarm.

questions.stem: The low-pressure alarm sounds on the ventilator of a sedated client who was just turned for skin care. The SpO2 is 93%. What should the nurse check first?

options.text: The tubing connections to the ventilator
The client's airway for thick secretions
Whether the client is biting on the tube
The client's sedation level and pain score

rationale.correct: Low pressure means air is escaping: check the connections, the circuit and the cuff.

perOption.a: A disconnection or leak, common after turning, is the most likely cause of a low-pressure alarm.
perOption.b: Secretions cause high-pressure alarms.
perOption.c: Biting causes high-pressure alarms.
perOption.d: This is not the first check for low pressure.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a low-pressure ventilator alarm.

questions.stem: A client's ventilator alarm sounds. The SpO2 is falling from 94% to 85%, the client looks distressed, and the nurse cannot quickly find the cause. Help has been called. What should the nurse do next?

options.text: Silence the alarm and wait for the respiratory therapist to arrive
Disconnect the ventilator and ventilate with a bag-valve device
Increase the ventilator's oxygen to 100% and watch the monitor
Remove the endotracheal tube so it can be replaced

rationale.correct: If the cause of a ventilator alarm cannot be found quickly and the client is in distress, ventilate manually with a bag-valve device.

perOption.a: The client needs ventilation now.
perOption.b: Manual ventilation supports the client while the problem is found.
perOption.c: This may not help if the problem is mechanical.
perOption.d: Only qualified providers reintubate, and the tube may be in place.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Support a ventilated client when the cause of an alarm is unknown.

questions.stem: The ICU nurse is planning care for a client on a ventilator for 3 days after aspiration pneumonia. Which actions help prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed at 30 to 45 degrees
Interrupt sedation daily and assess readiness to wean
Give oral care with a toothbrush on schedule
Drain tubing condensation away from the client
Keep the client flat to protect the sacrum
Change the ventilator circuit every day

rationale.correct: The VAP bundle includes head-of-bed elevation, daily sedation breaks, oral care and careful circuit management.

perOption.a: Elevation reduces aspiration of gastric contents.
perOption.b: Daily sedation breaks shorten ventilation time.
perOption.c: Oral care reduces bacteria that can be aspirated.
perOption.d: Draining toward the client can wash bacteria into the airway.
perOption.f: Circuits are changed only when soiled or malfunctioning.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia.

questions.stem: Right after a 60-year-old client with pneumonia is intubated in the emergency department, the nurse hears breath sounds over the right chest but none over the left. End-tidal CO2 is detected. What does this suggest?

options.text: The tube is correctly placed in the trachea
The tube is in the right mainstem bronchus
The tube is in the esophagus
The client has a left tension pneumothorax

rationale.correct: Confirm tube placement with end-tidal CO2, equal breath sounds and a chest x-ray.

perOption.a: Breath sounds should be equal on both sides.
perOption.b: The right bronchus is straighter, so a tube inserted too far tends to enter it and must be pulled back.
perOption.c: An esophageal tube gives no end-tidal CO2 and sounds over the stomach.
perOption.d: This is possible but much less likely right after intubation with these findings.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize right mainstem intubation.

questions.stem: A client with a tracheostomy has coarse rhonchi and an SpO2 of 91%. Place the steps for suctioning the tracheostomy in order, from first to last.

items.text: Perform hand hygiene and put on PPE
Apply intermittent suction while rotating and withdrawing, for 10 to 15 seconds at most
Re-oxygenate the client before another pass
Insert the catheter without applying suction

rationale.correct: Use sterile technique, pre-oxygenate, insert without suction, suction while withdrawing for no more than 15 seconds, then re-oxygenate.

perOption.a: Infection control comes first.
perOption.b: Pre-oxygenating reduces hypoxemia during suctioning.
perOption.c: Suction during insertion damages the mucosa and removes oxygen.
perOption.d: Limiting the time prevents hypoxemia.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Suction a tracheostomy safely.

questions.stem: A client had a tracheostomy placed this morning. Which items should be kept at the bedside?

options.text: Spare tubes (same size and smaller) and the obturator
A tongue blade, a penlight and a stethoscope at the head of the bed
A nasal cannula and an oxygen flow meter only
A urinary catheter kit and a bladder scanner

rationale.correct: Keep an obturator, spare tubes (same size and one smaller), suction equipment and a bag-valve device at the bedside.

perOption.a: These allow quick replacement if the tube comes out.
perOption.b: These are not essential for an airway emergency.
perOption.c: This is not enough for an airway emergency.
perOption.d: These are not related to airway safety.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prepare emergency equipment for a client with a tracheostomy.

questions.stem: The nurse checks the cuff pressure of a client's endotracheal tube during morning care and finds it is 45 cm H2O. The client is on a ventilator and has no audible air leak. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Leave the pressure as it is, since there is no air leak
Lower the cuff pressure to 20 to 30 cm H2O
Deflate the cuff fully so the trachea can rest
Add air until a small leak is heard on inspiration

rationale.correct: Keep cuff pressure at 20 to 30 cm H2O to prevent both aspiration and tracheal injury.

perOption.a: This pressure is high enough to cause tracheal ischemia.
perOption.b: This range seals the airway without cutting off blood flow to the tracheal mucosa.
perOption.c: A deflated cuff allows aspiration and loss of ventilation.
perOption.d: Adding air would raise the pressure further.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Maintain safe cuff pressure.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old client admitted 2 days ago with sepsis from pneumonia is receiving 80% oxygen by face mask. The PaO2 is 55 mm Hg, and the chest x-ray shows new bilateral infiltrates. An echocardiogram shows normal heart function, and the client has no history of heart disease. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Acute respiratory distress syndrome
Cardiogenic pulmonary edema
An acute asthma attack
Postoperative atelectasis

rationale.correct: ARDS shows hypoxemia that does not improve with oxygen and bilateral infiltrates without a cardiac cause.

perOption.a: Refractory hypoxemia with bilateral infiltrates after an insult such as sepsis, without heart failure, suggests ARDS.
perOption.b: The normal echocardiogram makes a cardiac cause unlikely.
perOption.c: Asthma does not cause bilateral infiltrates.
perOption.d: Atelectasis usually improves with oxygen and deep breathing.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize ARDS.

questions.stem: A client with severe ARDS on a ventilator is placed in the prone position for 16 hours a day. The family asks why. What is the purpose of this intervention?

options.text: To prevent pressure injuries on the back, buttocks and sacrum
To improve oxygenation by better matching air and blood flow
To make it easier to suction secretions from the airway
To reduce the amount of sedation the client needs

rationale.correct: Prone positioning recruits collapsed alveoli and improves oxygenation in moderate to severe ARDS.

perOption.a: Prone positioning increases pressure injury risk on the face and chest.
perOption.b: Prone positioning opens collapsed back regions of the lungs and improves oxygenation.
perOption.c: This is not the main purpose.
perOption.d: This is not the purpose.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Explain why prone positioning is used in ARDS.

questions.stem: In a restaurant, an adult is clutching the throat, cannot speak or cough, and is making high-pitched sounds. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Encourage the person to keep trying to cough
Give abdominal thrusts until the object comes out
Lay the person down and start chest compressions
Sweep the mouth with a finger to find the object

rationale.correct: Severe airway obstruction in a conscious adult: abdominal thrusts until the object comes out or the person becomes unresponsive.

perOption.a: Being unable to speak or cough means the obstruction is severe.
perOption.b: Abdominal thrusts are used for a conscious adult with a severe airway obstruction.
perOption.c: Compressions start only if the person becomes unresponsive.
perOption.d: Blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper.

references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Relieve a severe airway obstruction in a conscious adult.

questions.stem: An adult choking victim who was receiving abdominal thrusts becomes unresponsive. The nurse lowers the victim to the floor and calls for help. What should the nurse do next?

options.text: Keep giving abdominal thrusts with the victim lying on the floor
Begin CPR, looking in the mouth before each set of breaths
Sweep the mouth with a finger before doing anything else
Wait with the victim until the emergency team arrives

rationale.correct: For an unresponsive choking victim, start CPR and look in the mouth before giving breaths.

perOption.a: Once the victim is unresponsive, CPR is started instead.
perOption.b: Compressions can dislodge the object; it is removed only if it can be seen.
perOption.c: Blind sweeps are not recommended.
perOption.d: Delaying CPR worsens outcomes.

references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond when a choking victim becomes unresponsive.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old client had a left pneumonectomy for lung cancer this morning and has no chest tube. The client is alert and asks to lie on the right side to sleep. How should the nurse position the client?

options.text: On the right side, which the client has asked for
On the back or partly toward the operative side
Prone, with pillows under the chest and hips
Flat, with the head of the bed lowered fully

rationale.correct: After pneumonectomy, avoid lying fully on either side; position on the back or partly toward the operative side, per the surgeon's orders.

perOption.a: Lying fully on the remaining lung can shift the mediastinum and compress that lung.
perOption.b: This lets the remaining lung expand fully and avoids a mediastinal shift.
perOption.c: Prone positioning is not used after a pneumonectomy.
perOption.d: Lying flat reduces lung expansion.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A clinic nurse is reviewing four clients' charts for lung cancer screening eligibility. Which client meets the criteria for annual low-dose CT screening?

options.text: A 45-year-old who has smoked a pack a day for 25 years
A 62-year-old with 30 pack-years who quit 5 years ago
A 72-year-old with 40 pack-years who quit 25 years ago
A 58-year-old with 10 pack-years who still smokes

rationale.correct: USPSTF: annual low-dose CT for adults 50 to 80 with 20 or more pack-years who smoke now or quit within the past 15 years.

perOption.a: This client is younger than 50.
perOption.b: Screening is for adults 50 to 80 with 20 or more pack-years who smoke now or quit within 15 years.
perOption.c: Quitting more than 15 years ago puts this client outside the criteria.
perOption.d: This history is under 20 pack-years.

references: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify clients who meet lung cancer screening criteria.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old client reports smoking 1.5 packs of cigarettes a day for 30 years and quitting last year. The nurse is checking eligibility for lung cancer screening. How many pack-years is this?

rationale.correct: Pack-years = packs per day × years smoked = 1.5 × 30 = 45 pack-years.
references: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Calculate a smoking history in pack-years.

questions.stem: A client with obstructive sleep apnea and a body mass index of 38 has been prescribed CPAP at night. Which statement by the client shows understanding?

options.text: "I'll use it on nights when I feel especially tired."
"I'll wear it whenever I sleep, even for naps."
"I'll take a sleeping pill to help me get used to the mask."
"I'll stop using it if the mask leaks around my nose."

rationale.correct: CPAP works only when used for all sleep; avoid alcohol and sedatives.

perOption.a: CPAP must be used every night to work.
perOption.b: Consistent use keeps the airway open during all sleep.
perOption.c: Sedatives worsen airway collapse in sleep apnea.
perOption.d: Mask problems are fixed, not a reason to stop.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach CPAP use for sleep apnea.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old client with three fractured ribs is taking shallow breaths because of pain and has diminished breath sounds at the bases. Which intervention is most important to prevent complications?

options.text: Wrap the chest snugly with an elastic binder for support
Give enough pain relief to allow deep breaths
Keep the client on bed rest until the pain improves
Limit fluids to reduce the work of breathing

rationale.correct: Pain control and deep breathing prevent atelectasis and pneumonia after rib fractures.

perOption.a: Binding the chest limits expansion and raises the risk of pneumonia.
perOption.b: Pain control allows deep breathing and coughing, preventing atelectasis and pneumonia.
perOption.c: Immobility increases respiratory complications.
perOption.d: Limiting fluids thickens secretions.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prevent pulmonary complications after rib fractures.
